payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage

———

Source A
Fewer Buses, Longer Days: Harrow Fork Finishes Its First Four-Day Year
Tobias Lindqvist, staff reporter, The Cobble Creek Ledger, 2024

The last yellow bus of the school year pulled out of the Harrow Fork Consolidated Schools lot on a Thursday afternoon, which is now the end of the week here. When the district of about 1,900 students adopted a four-day calendar last August, it became the fourth in the county to do so. The school day grew by 55 minutes, Friday became a day off for students, and administrators promised that the money and the teachers would follow.

On the money, the district's own figures show a savings of roughly 410,000 dollars, close to 2 percent of its operating budget, most of it from parking the bus fleet one day a week. On teachers, the change is harder to measure but easier to feel. The district opened the previous year with 14 unfilled teaching positions. It opened this one with 5.

Not everyone is counting the same things. The public library doubled its Friday staffing and still turned away children when its community room filled. Two of the three day-care centers in town added a Friday rate. A spring survey conducted by the district found that teachers overwhelmingly want to keep the schedule, while parents of elementary students are nearly split.

The school board will vote in July on whether to renew the calendar for a second year. "We said we'd look at the numbers honestly," board chair Everett Mbanefo said at the May meeting. "That means the reading scores and the day-care bills, not just the bus budget."

———

Source B
Friday Is Not a Gift If You Have to Pay for It
Marisol Ettinger, guest column, The Cobble Creek Ledger, 2024

I own the hardware store on Dunmore Street, and I have two kids at Harrow Fork Elementary. Since August, every Friday has been a math problem. My husband drives for a feed supplier and cannot take the day. I open at seven. So either my eight-year-old sits in the back room with a tablet for nine hours, or I pay the day-care center's new Friday rate, which comes to 38 dollars a child. That is 76 dollars a week, more than 2,700 dollars across the school year, for a schedule I never asked for.

Supporters keep telling me what the district saved. I believe them. But a saving that moves from the district's ledger to mine is not a saving; it is a transfer, and it lands hardest on the families least able to absorb it. The parents who cheered loudest at the board meeting tend to have a grandparent down the road or a job they can do from a kitchen table. Plenty of us have neither.

I also notice who has been quiet. The high school students love it, of course. Ask a sixteen-year-old whether she wants a three-day weekend and you already know the answer. The younger children do not get a vote, and they are the ones whose reading teachers now have 55 more minutes a day to fill with children who, by two o'clock, are done.

If the board wants to keep teachers, it should pay them. Raise the levy, cut something else, say so plainly. Do not hand the bill to the families in the lunch line and call it a gift.

———

Source C
Three Years In: A Conversation with Superintendent Ruth Castellane of Pinemont Valley Unified
Interview conducted by Devin Achterberg, Pinemont Valley Education Review, 2023

Achterberg: Pinemont Valley has been on a four-day calendar for three years. What did you expect, and what actually happened?

Castellane: I expected a budget story. We did save money, about 1.5 percent of operations, but that turned out to be the least important thing. What changed was hiring. The year before we switched, we posted a middle school science job and got two applications, one from a man who later withdrew. Last spring the same posting drew eleven. Teachers in the region now ask about our calendar before they ask about our salary schedule.

Achterberg: Critics say the day off comes at the expense of younger students.

Castellane: They are partly right, and I would rather say so than pretend otherwise. We tracked it. Our third and fourth graders lost ground in reading the first year, not dramatically, but measurably. We responded by moving reading to the first block of the morning and adding a paid Friday tutoring session for anyone below grade level. Second and third year, the gap closed. I would not recommend the calendar to any district that is not willing to do that kind of repair work.

Achterberg: What about families who need Friday care?

Castellane: That is the hardest part, and I will not dress it up. We run a Friday enrichment day at two of our five buildings, staffed by aides and paid for mostly by a county grant. It serves about 140 children. It does not serve everyone. If a district tells you it has solved the childcare problem, ask to see the waiting list.

Achterberg: Would you go back?

Castellane: No. But I also would not have voted for it on the information we had at the time. We got lucky, and then we worked.

———

Source D
Four-Day Calendars in Rural Districts: Three-Year Findings
Research brief, Meridian Basin Institute for Rural Education Policy (a fictional policy research center), 2025

This brief summarizes three years of records from 23 districts in the Meridian Basin region that adopted a four-day instructional calendar between 2021 and 2023, compared with 31 neighboring districts that retained five days.

Fiscal effects. Reported savings ranged from 1.2 to 2.5 percent of annual operating budgets, concentrated in transportation, utilities and substitute pay. No district achieved the 5 percent savings that several had projected before adoption, chiefly because salaries, the largest cost, are unaffected by the number of days taught.

Achievement. Outcomes depended on what districts did with the lost day. In the 9 districts that lengthened the remaining four days enough to preserve total instructional hours, achievement growth in reading and mathematics was statistically indistinguishable from the comparison districts. In the 14 districts that accepted a net reduction in hours, mathematics growth over three years trailed comparison districts by an average of 3 percentile points, with the largest effects in grades 2 through 5.

Staffing. Four-day districts reported a median of 2.4 times as many applicants per certified vacancy in year three as in the year before adoption. Comparison districts saw no comparable change. Teacher attrition fell in 18 of the 23 districts.

Families. In household surveys, 41 percent of parents of children under age 12 reported new weekly childcare costs attributable to the calendar; 22 percent reported reducing their own work hours. Reported benefits included more time for medical appointments and reduced family travel for extracurricular events.

Recommendation. The evidence does not support a blanket endorsement or rejection. Districts considering the calendar should commit in advance to preserving instructional hours, funding a fifth-day option for younger children, and reviewing achievement data publicly after two years.

———

Source E (table)
Should Harrow Fork Keep the Four-Day Calendar? Survey Results by Group
Spring 2024 community survey, Harrow Fork Consolidated Schools, 1,112 responses

The table reports responses to a survey conducted by Harrow Fork Consolidated Schools in April 2024 asking whether the district should keep its four-day calendar for a second year. Figures are percentages of respondents within each group, and each row sums to 100.

| Respondent group | Keep it (%) | Return to five days (%) | Unsure (%) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Teachers | 84 | 9 | 7 |
| Support staff (bus drivers, aides, custodians) | 58 | 31 | 11 |
| Parents of elementary students | 48 | 42 | 10 |
| Parents of middle and high school students | 63 | 27 | 10 |
| Students in grades 9 through 12 | 79 | 12 | 9 |
| Local employers | 37 | 49 | 14 |

———

Source F (chart)
Where Harrow Fork's First-Year Savings Came From
Chart prepared from the Harrow Fork Consolidated Schools year-end budget summary, 2024

parts.prompt:
A growing number of small and mid-sized school districts have shortened the school week to four days, usually by lengthening each remaining day and giving students Fridays off. Supporters point to budget savings, easier teacher recruitment, and more family time. Opponents point to childcare costs, lost instructional time for young children, and uneven effects across households. Some observers argue the schedule can work only under specific conditions. Carefully read the six sources that follow, including the introductory information for each source.

Write an essay that synthesizes material from at least three of the sources and develops your position on whether a school district should move to a four-day school week.

Your essay should:
- Take a clear, defensible position on whether, or under what conditions, a district should adopt a four-day week; a conditional or qualified position is acceptable if it is clearly stated and consistently developed.
- Use material from at least three of the six sources to support your line of reasoning, and identify each source you use as Source A, Source B, Source C, Source D, Source E, or Source F.
- Explain how each piece of evidence supports your reasoning; do not simply summarize or list the sources.
- Treat the sources as material for your own argument rather than as the argument itself; you may agree with, challenge, or qualify what a source claims.
parts.model_answer:
When people argue about the four-day school week, they usually argue about Fridays. Teachers and teenagers picture a three-day weekend, and working parents picture a day-care bill. But the real question for a district isn't whether Fridays off are good or bad. It's who ends up paying for them. A district should move to a four-day week only if it will do two things before the first Thursday dismissal: lengthen the remaining days enough to keep total instructional hours the same, and pay for a Friday option for children under twelve. If it can't afford both, it should find another way to fix its teacher shortage.

The case for the schedule is not really about money, even though money is what gets announced. Harrow Fork saved about 410,000, dollars "close to 2 percent of its operating budget" (Source A), and Source D found that savings across 23 districts topped out at 2.5 percent, with none reaching the 5 percent some had promised. Source F shows why. The biggest savings come from parking buses (165,000 dollars) and paying for fewer utilities, and there is no bar for teacher salaries at all, because teachers get paid the same whether school meets four days or five. A district hoping to balance its budget this way will be disappointed. What it can realistically buy is teachers. Harrow Fork went from 14 unfilled positions to 5 (Source A), Pinemont Valley's science posting went from two applications to eleven (Source C), and across the Meridian Basin applicants per vacancy rose 2.4 times (Source D). That is the same pattern at the scale of one job, one district, and a whole region, which makes it hard to dismiss as luck. For a rural district that can't find a science teacher, this is a serious argument.

The problem is that the hiring benefit goes to the district while the cost goes somewhere else. Marisol Ettinger, a store owner with two kids in elementary school, pays 76 dollars a week, over 2,700 dollars a year, for Friday care, and she argues that "a saving that moves from the district's ledger to mine is not a saving; it is a transfer" (Source B). It would be easy to write her off as one frustrated parent, except that Source D found 41 percent of parents of children under 12 reported new childcare costs and 22 percent cut their own work hours. Source E shows the same split: 84 percent of teachers want to keep the calendar, but elementary parents are divided 48 to 42, and local employers, probably the people covering for those parents' missing hours, oppose it 49 to 37. The groups who like the schedule most are the ones it was designed to help, and the people closest to the youngest children are the ones paying for it.

That is why the conditions matter. Source D's achievement findings suggest the four-day schedule isn't the problem; lost hours are. Districts that kept total hours saw growth "statistically indistinguishable" from five-day districts, while those that cut hours fell 3 percentile points behind in math, mostly in grades 2 through 5. Pinemont Valley's third and fourth graders slipped in reading the first year, and the gap only closed after the district moved reading to the morning and paid for Friday tutoring (Source C). So a first-year dip doesn't prove the schedule fails, but a closed gap doesn't prove it works by itself either. Castellane's own summary, "We got lucky, and then we worked," reads less like a success story than a warning.

Even Pinemont hasn't solved childcare. Its enrichment day serves about 140 children at two of five buildings, paid for mostly by a county grant, and Castellane tells critics to "ask to see the waiting list." A district without that grant is not Pinemont. Harrow Fork has a library turning children away on Fridays and day-cares adding new rates, which suggests the town absorbed the cost instead of the district planning for it. Before a board copies Pinemont's results, it should ask whether it can copy Pinemont's repair work.

The four-day week is not a budget fix, and it is not a gift. It's a trade: teachers in exchange for a Friday that someone has to cover. A district that pays for that Friday itself has made a fair trade. A district that can't should take Source B's advice, raise the levy and pay teachers directly, because at least that puts the cost where everyone can see it.

Count as 'using' a source only when the writer draws a specific claim, figure, or example from it and attributes it (Source A through Source F). Numbers from Source E or Source F count as evidence when the writer interprets them (for example, that employers oppose the schedule while teachers favor it, and why that gap matters), not when they are simply reproduced. Source C and Source D can be used for more than one stance; credit depends on the writer's explanation, not on which stance the writer takes.

Sophistication is not earned by taking the middle stance automatically. A conditional thesis with vague conditions is no more sophisticated than a one-sided essay; a one-sided essay that honestly confronts Source C's caveats or Source B's cost-transfer logic can earn the point.

Scoring guide (ALTON practice rubric, not official College Board scoring). Each essay is worth 6 points.
Thesis (0-1): A conditional thesis earns the point only if the conditions are named, not merely gestured at ('it depends on the district'). A thesis that says the schedule 'has pros and cons' without resolving them does not earn the point.
   - 1: States a defensible position on whether, or under what conditions, a district should move to a four-day week. The position may be unconditional (adopt / do not adopt), conditional (adopt only if instructional hours are preserved and a fifth-day option is funded), or alternative (reject the schedule and address teacher shortages another way). A thesis may appear anywhere in the essay and may be more than one sentence, but it must commit to a stance the rest of the essay can defend.

Evidence and commentary (0-4): Count as 'using' a source only when the writer draws a specific claim, figure, or example from it and attributes it (Source A through Source F). Numbers from Source E or Source F count as evidence when the writer interprets them (for example, that employers oppose the schedule while teachers favor it, and why that gap matters), not when they are simply reproduced. Source C and Source D can be used for more than one stance; credit depends on the writer's explanation, not on which stance the writer takes.
   - 4: Uses at least three sources with well-chosen, specific evidence throughout and consistently explains how each piece advances the argument. Sources are synthesized rather than stacked: the writer notices, for example, that Source A's reduction in vacancies, Source C's eleven applicants, and Source D's 2.4 multiplier describe the same phenomenon at three scales, or that Source E's split among elementary parents matches the grade-level findings in Source D. The essay engages with evidence that complicates its position and explains why the position still holds.
   - 3: Uses at least three sources with specific, accurate evidence and explains how most of it supports a clear line of reasoning. The writer may put two sources in conversation (for instance, Source B's cost-transfer argument against Source F's breakdown of savings) but one or two pieces of evidence may be underexplained, or the essay may not account for the strongest counter-evidence.
   - 2: Uses at least three sources but commentary is thin or repetitive: the writer quotes or paraphrases a figure (such as the 410,000 dollar savings or the 41 percent childcare figure) and then asserts that it proves the point without explaining why. Evidence may be loosely connected to the thesis, or the essay may treat each source in isolation without connecting them.
   - 1: Mostly summary or paraphrase of fewer than three sources, or of three sources with no explanation of how any of them supports the writer's position. Sources may be mentioned in a list ('Sources A, C, and D all discuss savings') without being put to use.
   - 0: Restates the thesis, offers only personal opinion with no source material, or uses sources in a way that shows misreading (for example, claiming Source D proves four-day weeks raise test scores).
Sophistication (0-1): Sophistication is not earned by taking the middle stance automatically. A conditional thesis with vague conditions is no more sophisticated than a one-sided essay; a one-sided essay that honestly confronts Source C's caveats or Source B's cost-transfer logic can earn the point.
   - 1: Demonstrates a complex understanding of the issue through one or more of the following, carried through the essay rather than appearing in a single sentence: explaining why the same evidence (such as the modest 2 percent savings) can support opposing conclusions; identifying who gains and who pays and treating that distribution as central to the decision; recognizing that Harrow Fork and Pinemont Valley are different districts and reasoning about whether one's experience transfers to another; distinguishing between short-run effects (first-year reading dips) and long-run effects (closed gaps after repair work); or making a conditional argument whose conditions are drawn from and tested against the sources.
   - 0: Argument stays at a general level ('the district should weigh costs and benefits'), relies on vague praise or blame, uses ornamental but empty language, or acknowledges a counterargument only to drop it.
Note: Scores are additive: Row A (0-1) plus Row B (0-4) plus Row C (0-1), maximum 6.
Note: An essay that earns 0 on Row A can still earn up to 2 on Row B if it uses sources, but cannot earn 3 or 4 because there is no position for the evidence to support.
Note: Misstating a figure from a source (for example, calling the savings 5 percent) counts against accuracy on Row B; one small slip does not by itself lower the score, but a pattern does.
Note: Writers who cite Source E or Source F must interpret the numbers; an essay that reproduces the table as a sentence earns no more credit than one that mentions the source by letter.
Note: Essays that reject the four-day week and propose a different remedy for teacher shortages (such as Source B's levy proposal) are fully defensible, provided the writer still engages with the sources' evidence on the schedule itself.

Sample response, middle score (4/6; Thesis 1, Evidence and commentary 3, Sophistication 0):
A school district should only move to a four-day week if it is willing to keep the same number of instructional hours and provide care for families on Fridays. Without those two things, the schedule saves a little money but costs students and parents too much.

The main reason districts do this is money and teachers, and the sources show both benefits are real but small or uneven. In Source A, Harrow Fork saved about 410,000 dollars, which is close to 2 percent of its budget. Source F shows that most of this came from transportation and utilities, and none of it came from teacher salaries. That means the savings are not very big, since salaries are the biggest cost. Source D agrees, saying no district reached the 5 percent that some expected. So if a district is only doing this to save money, it is probably not worth it.

The better argument for the four-day week is hiring teachers. Source A says Harrow Fork went from 14 unfilled positions to 5, and Source C says Pinemont Valley got eleven applicants for a job that used to get two. Source D also found that four-day districts had 2.4 times as many applicants. These all show that teachers like the schedule, which is also shown in Source E where 84 percent of teachers want to keep it. This is a strong point in favor of the schedule, because a district with empty classrooms has a serious problem.

However, the schedule has real downsides for younger kids and for families. Source D says districts that cut total hours had math scores that fell behind by 3 percentile points, especially in grades 2 through 5. Source C backs this up because third and fourth graders lost ground in reading the first year. The Pinemont superintendent fixed it with tutoring, but that took extra effort and money. This is why I think a district must keep its hours up. Families also pay. Source B describes a parent paying 76 dollars a week for day care, and Source D says 41 percent of parents of young children had new childcare costs. Source E shows elementary parents are split, 48 percent to 42 percent, while local employers mostly want to go back, which shows that the people who feel the cost are not happy.

Some people might say the teacher hiring is more important than the childcare costs. That is a fair point, but a savings that just moves the cost to parents, as Source B says, is not really a savings. Pinemont Valley also says they "got lucky, and then we worked," so other districts should not assume it will go the same way for them.

In conclusion, a district should adopt the four-day week only with preserved hours, a funded Friday option for young children, and a plan to check the results. If it cannot do those things, it should keep five days and find another way to pay teachers.

   - "Source F shows that most of this came from transportation and utilities, and none of it came from teacher salaries." - Accurate and interpreted. The writer connects the chart to why savings are limited, and ties it to Source D. This is one of the stronger moments of synthesis.
   - "These all show that teachers like the schedule, which is also shown in Source E where 84 percent of teachers want to keep it." - Source A, C and D are grouped as describing hiring, but the commentary slips to 'teachers like the schedule' and does not explain that these are the same phenomenon at different scales. Source E's figure is mostly reproduced.
   - "Source E shows elementary parents are split, 48 percent to 42 percent, while local employers mostly want to go back, which shows that the people who feel the cost are not happy." - Interprets Source E somewhat, but the link to Source D's grade-level findings is not made and the commentary stays general.
   - "Source B describes a parent paying 76 dollars a week for day care, and Source D says 41 percent of parents of young children had new childcare costs." - Accurate figures from two sources, but they are placed side by side with little explanation of how the anecdote and the survey strengthen each other.

The four day school week is a big decision for any district and there are a lot of opinions about it. Some people like it and some people do not. In this essay I will look at both sides and talk about what the sources say.

Source A is about Harrow Fork which switched to four days. The district saved about 410,000 dollars and went from 14 unfilled teaching jobs to 5. That is a lot of money and it shows the four day week works for the budget. But the same article says day care centers added a Friday rate so not everyone is happy.

Source B is written by a mom who owns a hardware store. She says she has to pay 38 dollars a child for Friday day care which is 76 dollars a week. This shows that the four day week costs families money. She also says younger kids get tired by two o'clock. I think this is a good point because little kids cannot focus that long.

Source D is a research brief that looked at 23 districts. It says savings were between 1.2 and 2.5 percent and that 41 percent of parents had new childcare costs. It also says math scores went down in some districts. So the four day week has good things and bad things.

In conclusion, the four day week has pros and cons. Districts should think carefully about the money and the students and the families before they decide. If they do that they can make the right choice for their district.

sources.title: Fewer Buses, Longer Days: Harrow Fork Finishes Its First Four-Day Year
sources.attribution: Tobias Lindqvist, staff reporter, The Cobble Creek Ledger, 2024
sources.body:
The last yellow bus of the school year pulled out of the Harrow Fork Consolidated Schools lot on a Thursday afternoon, which is now the end of the week here. When the district of about 1,900 students adopted a four-day calendar last August, it became the fourth in the county to do so. The school day grew by 55 minutes, Friday became a day off for students, and administrators promised that the money and the teachers would follow.

On the money, the district's own figures show a savings of roughly 410,000 dollars, close to 2 percent of its operating budget, most of it from parking the bus fleet one day a week. On teachers, the change is harder to measure but easier to feel. The district opened the previous year with 14 unfilled teaching positions. It opened this one with 5.

Not everyone is counting the same things. The public library doubled its Friday staffing and still turned away children when its community room filled. Two of the three day-care centers in town added a Friday rate. A spring survey conducted by the district found that teachers overwhelmingly want to keep the schedule, while parents of elementary students are nearly split.

The school board will vote in July on whether to renew the calendar for a second year. "We said we'd look at the numbers honestly," board chair Everett Mbanefo said at the May meeting. "That means the reading scores and the day-care bills, not just the bus budget."

sources.title: Friday Is Not a Gift If You Have to Pay for It
sources.attribution: Marisol Ettinger, guest column, The Cobble Creek Ledger, 2024
sources.body:
I own the hardware store on Dunmore Street, and I have two kids at Harrow Fork Elementary. Since August, every Friday has been a math problem. My husband drives for a feed supplier and cannot take the day. I open at seven. So either my eight-year-old sits in the back room with a tablet for nine hours, or I pay the day-care center's new Friday rate, which comes to 38 dollars a child. That is 76 dollars a week, more than 2,700 dollars across the school year, for a schedule I never asked for.

Supporters keep telling me what the district saved. I believe them. But a saving that moves from the district's ledger to mine is not a saving; it is a transfer, and it lands hardest on the families least able to absorb it. The parents who cheered loudest at the board meeting tend to have a grandparent down the road or a job they can do from a kitchen table. Plenty of us have neither.

I also notice who has been quiet. The high school students love it, of course. Ask a sixteen-year-old whether she wants a three-day weekend and you already know the answer. The younger children do not get a vote, and they are the ones whose reading teachers now have 55 more minutes a day to fill with children who, by two o'clock, are done.

If the board wants to keep teachers, it should pay them. Raise the levy, cut something else, say so plainly. Do not hand the bill to the families in the lunch line and call it a gift.

sources.title: Three Years In: A Conversation with Superintendent Ruth Castellane of Pinemont Valley Unified
sources.attribution: Interview conducted by Devin Achterberg, Pinemont Valley Education Review, 2023
sources.body:
Achterberg: Pinemont Valley has been on a four-day calendar for three years. What did you expect, and what actually happened?

Castellane: I expected a budget story. We did save money, about 1.5 percent of operations, but that turned out to be the least important thing. What changed was hiring. The year before we switched, we posted a middle school science job and got two applications, one from a man who later withdrew. Last spring the same posting drew eleven. Teachers in the region now ask about our calendar before they ask about our salary schedule.

Achterberg: Critics say the day off comes at the expense of younger students.

Castellane: They are partly right, and I would rather say so than pretend otherwise. We tracked it. Our third and fourth graders lost ground in reading the first year, not dramatically, but measurably. We responded by moving reading to the first block of the morning and adding a paid Friday tutoring session for anyone below grade level. Second and third year, the gap closed. I would not recommend the calendar to any district that is not willing to do that kind of repair work.

Achterberg: What about families who need Friday care?

Castellane: That is the hardest part, and I will not dress it up. We run a Friday enrichment day at two of our five buildings, staffed by aides and paid for mostly by a county grant. It serves about 140 children. It does not serve everyone. If a district tells you it has solved the childcare problem, ask to see the waiting list.

Achterberg: Would you go back?

Castellane: No. But I also would not have voted for it on the information we had at the time. We got lucky, and then we worked.

sources.title: Four-Day Calendars in Rural Districts: Three-Year Findings
sources.attribution: Research brief, Meridian Basin Institute for Rural Education Policy (a fictional policy research center), 2025
sources.body:
This brief summarizes three years of records from 23 districts in the Meridian Basin region that adopted a four-day instructional calendar between 2021 and 2023, compared with 31 neighboring districts that retained five days.

Fiscal effects. Reported savings ranged from 1.2 to 2.5 percent of annual operating budgets, concentrated in transportation, utilities and substitute pay. No district achieved the 5 percent savings that several had projected before adoption, chiefly because salaries, the largest cost, are unaffected by the number of days taught.

Achievement. Outcomes depended on what districts did with the lost day. In the 9 districts that lengthened the remaining four days enough to preserve total instructional hours, achievement growth in reading and mathematics was statistically indistinguishable from the comparison districts. In the 14 districts that accepted a net reduction in hours, mathematics growth over three years trailed comparison districts by an average of 3 percentile points, with the largest effects in grades 2 through 5.

Staffing. Four-day districts reported a median of 2.4 times as many applicants per certified vacancy in year three as in the year before adoption. Comparison districts saw no comparable change. Teacher attrition fell in 18 of the 23 districts.

Families. In household surveys, 41 percent of parents of children under age 12 reported new weekly childcare costs attributable to the calendar; 22 percent reported reducing their own work hours. Reported benefits included more time for medical appointments and reduced family travel for extracurricular events.

Recommendation. The evidence does not support a blanket endorsement or rejection. Districts considering the calendar should commit in advance to preserving instructional hours, funding a fifth-day option for younger children, and reviewing achievement data publicly after two years.

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No thesis; a thesis that only restates the prompt (for example, 'There are many opinions about the four-day week'); a thesis that merely lists what the sources say without taking a position; or a thesis that answers a different question (such as whether teachers deserve raises) without connecting it to whether a district should adopt the schedule.
descriptors.1: States a defensible position on whether, or under what conditions, a district should move to a four-day week. The position may be unconditional (adopt / do not adopt), conditional (adopt only if instructional hours are preserved and a fifth-day option is funded), or alternative (reject the schedule and address teacher shortages another way). A thesis may appear anywhere in the essay and may be more than one sentence, but it must commit to a stance the rest of the essay can defend.

rows.task_specific: A conditional thesis earns the point only if the conditions are named, not merely gestured at ('it depends on the district'). A thesis that says the schedule 'has pros and cons' without resolving them does not earn the point.

rows.name: Evidence and commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis, offers only personal opinion with no source material, or uses sources in a way that shows misreading (for example, claiming Source D proves four-day weeks raise test scores).
descriptors.1: Mostly summary or paraphrase of fewer than three sources, or of three sources with no explanation of how any of them supports the writer's position. Sources may be mentioned in a list ('Sources A, C, and D all discuss savings') without being put to use.
descriptors.2: Uses at least three sources but commentary is thin or repetitive: the writer quotes or paraphrases a figure (such as the 410,000 dollar savings or the 41 percent childcare figure) and then asserts that it proves the point without explaining why. Evidence may be loosely connected to the thesis, or the essay may treat each source in isolation without connecting them.
descriptors.3: Uses at least three sources with specific, accurate evidence and explains how most of it supports a clear line of reasoning. The writer may put two sources in conversation (for instance, Source B's cost-transfer argument against Source F's breakdown of savings) but one or two pieces of evidence may be underexplained, or the essay may not account for the strongest counter-evidence.
descriptors.4: Uses at least three sources with well-chosen, specific evidence throughout and consistently explains how each piece advances the argument. Sources are synthesized rather than stacked: the writer notices, for example, that Source A's reduction in vacancies, Source C's eleven applicants, and Source D's 2.4 multiplier describe the same phenomenon at three scales, or that Source E's split among elementary parents matches the grade-level findings in Source D. The essay engages with evidence that complicates its position and explains why the position still holds.

rows.task_specific: Count as 'using' a source only when the writer draws a specific claim, figure, or example from it and attributes it (Source A through Source F). Numbers from Source E or Source F count as evidence when the writer interprets them (for example, that employers oppose the schedule while teachers favor it, and why that gap matters), not when they are simply reproduced. Source C and Source D can be used for more than one stance; credit depends on the writer's explanation, not on which stance the writer takes.

rows.name: Sophistication

descriptors.0: Argument stays at a general level ('the district should weigh costs and benefits'), relies on vague praise or blame, uses ornamental but empty language, or acknowledges a counterargument only to drop it.
descriptors.1: Demonstrates a complex understanding of the issue through one or more of the following, carried through the essay rather than appearing in a single sentence: explaining why the same evidence (such as the modest 2 percent savings) can support opposing conclusions; identifying who gains and who pays and treating that distribution as central to the decision; recognizing that Harrow Fork and Pinemont Valley are different districts and reasoning about whether one's experience transfers to another; distinguishing between short-run effects (first-year reading dips) and long-run effects (closed gaps after repair work); or making a conditional argument whose conditions are drawn from and tested against the sources.

rows.task_specific: Sophistication is not earned by taking the middle stance automatically. A conditional thesis with vague conditions is no more sophisticated than a one-sided essay; a one-sided essay that honestly confronts Source C's caveats or Source B's cost-transfer logic can earn the point.

scoring_notes: Scores are additive: Row A (0-1) plus Row B (0-4) plus Row C (0-1), maximum 6.
An essay that earns 0 on Row A can still earn up to 2 on Row B if it uses sources, but cannot earn 3 or 4 because there is no position for the evidence to support.
Misstating a figure from a source (for example, calling the savings 5 percent) counts against accuracy on Row B; one small slip does not by itself lower the score, but a pattern does.
Writers who cite Source E or Source F must interpret the numbers; an essay that reproduces the table as a sentence earns no more credit than one that mentions the source by letter.

Essays that reject the four-day week and propose a different remedy for teacher shortages (such as Source B's levy proposal) are fully defensible, provided the writer still engages with the sources' evidence on the schedule itself.

defensible_positions: Adopt the four-day week: the hiring and retention gains (Sources A, C, D) address the most serious problem small districts face, and the drawbacks are manageable with planning.

Reject the four-day week: savings are small and operational (Sources D, F), while costs are shifted to families and young children (Sources B, D, E); teacher shortages should be addressed through pay instead.

Adopt only under conditions: preserve total instructional hours, fund a fifth-day program for younger children, and commit to a public data review (Sources C, D), with Harrow Fork's split survey (Source E) showing what happens when those conditions are not in place.

Pilot before deciding: run the schedule in secondary schools only, where support is strongest (Source E) and achievement effects are smallest (Source D), while keeping elementary schools on five days.

Decide based on who pays: the schedule is justified only where a district can prevent the cost transfer Source B describes; where it cannot, the hiring gains do not outweigh the harm to the families least able to absorb it.
lines_of_reasoning: Chain the staffing evidence across scales (Source A vacancies falling from 14 to 5, Source C's two applicants becoming eleven, Source D's 2.4 multiplier) to argue that recruitment, not savings, is the real case for the schedule.
Use Source F and Source D together to show that savings are structurally limited, then use Source B to argue that even those limited savings are partly a transfer to households.
Use Source D's hours-preserved versus hours-reduced split, plus Source C's reading dip and recovery, to argue that the achievement question is really a design question.
Read Source E as a map of winners and losers: those with the most control over the decision (teachers, older students) favor it; those with the least (elementary parents, employers) do not.
Argue from Source C's own caution ('I would not have voted for it on the information we had') that a district without a repair plan and a Friday program should not proceed.

rhetorical_choices.effect: In Source B, setting 'saving' against 'transfer' reframes the district's fiscal claim as a question of who pays, which writers can adopt or contest.
In Source B, the sixteen-year-old question dismisses student enthusiasm as predictable, inviting writers to weigh whose preferences in Source E should count.
In Source C, the superintendent concedes the critics are 'partly right' before describing repair work, modeling the conditional stance and giving writers a credible insider's caveat.
In Source D, the refusal of a 'blanket endorsement or rejection' pushes writers toward naming specific conditions rather than taking a general stance.
In Source A, the two short sentences on vacancies (14, then 5) make the staffing gain vivid without editorializing, a figure writers on any side must account for.

source_uses.usable_for: Concrete first-year picture of one district: 410,000 dollars saved (about 2 percent), vacancies dropping from 14 to 5, library and day-care strain, and a board chair's insistence on looking at reading scores and day-care bills; usable by every stance as a balanced case study.

The strongest objection: savings are a cost transfer to families (38 dollars per child per Friday, about 2,700 dollars a year), younger children lose the most, and the alternative is to pay teachers directly; usable to oppose, or to define the conditions a conditional stance must meet.

An experienced supporter's testimony: hiring improved sharply, early reading losses were real but repaired with morning reading blocks and Friday tutoring, Friday care serves only 140 children; usable for adoption, for conditions, or (through her own caution) for skepticism.

Comparative evidence across 23 districts: savings between 1.2 and 2.5 percent, achievement unaffected where hours were preserved but 3 percentile points lower in math where they were not, 2.4 times as many applicants, 41 percent of parents of young children facing new costs; usable for any stance, and essential for conditional arguments.

Group-by-group support in Harrow Fork: teachers 84 percent, high school students 79 percent, elementary parents 48 percent, employers 37 percent; usable to show that support tracks who benefits, or to argue that a majority of most groups favor keeping it.

Breakdown of the 410,000 dollars: transportation 165 thousand, utilities 95, substitutes 80, food service 45, other 25, with no salary savings; usable to show savings are real but structurally modest and operational, confirming Source D's explanation.

common_pitfalls: Treating the essay as a report on the sources ('Source A says, Source B says') rather than an argument that uses them.

Citing the 410,000 dollar figure from Source A or Source F as if it settled the fiscal question without noting Source D's finding that savings are capped near 2.5 percent because salaries are untouched.
Reading Source D as uniformly negative or uniformly positive; its achievement findings depend on whether instructional hours were preserved, and essays that miss the distinction misuse the source.
Assuming Source C and Source A describe the same district; Pinemont Valley and Harrow Fork are different places with different years of experience.
Using Source E only to say 'most people support it' when the table shows sharp differences among groups, especially between teachers and elementary parents or employers.
Dismissing Source B as 'just one parent' instead of engaging with the argument that savings have been transferred rather than eliminated.
Writing a conditional thesis ('it depends on the district') without specifying which conditions and then defending them with evidence.
Ignoring the question of who bears the costs; many weak essays argue about whether the schedule 'works' without asking for whom.

samples.essay:
When people argue about the four-day school week, they usually argue about Fridays. Teachers and teenagers picture a three-day weekend, and working parents picture a day-care bill. But the real question for a district isn't whether Fridays off are good or bad. It's who ends up paying for them. A district should move to a four-day week only if it will do two things before the first Thursday dismissal: lengthen the remaining days enough to keep total instructional hours the same, and pay for a Friday option for children under twelve. If it can't afford both, it should find another way to fix its teacher shortage.

The case for the schedule is not really about money, even though money is what gets announced. Harrow Fork saved about 410,000, dollars "close to 2 percent of its operating budget" (Source A), and Source D found that savings across 23 districts topped out at 2.5 percent, with none reaching the 5 percent some had promised. Source F shows why. The biggest savings come from parking buses (165,000 dollars) and paying for fewer utilities, and there is no bar for teacher salaries at all, because teachers get paid the same whether school meets four days or five. A district hoping to balance its budget this way will be disappointed. What it can realistically buy is teachers. Harrow Fork went from 14 unfilled positions to 5 (Source A), Pinemont Valley's science posting went from two applications to eleven (Source C), and across the Meridian Basin applicants per vacancy rose 2.4 times (Source D). That is the same pattern at the scale of one job, one district, and a whole region, which makes it hard to dismiss as luck. For a rural district that can't find a science teacher, this is a serious argument.

The problem is that the hiring benefit goes to the district while the cost goes somewhere else. Marisol Ettinger, a store owner with two kids in elementary school, pays 76 dollars a week, over 2,700 dollars a year, for Friday care, and she argues that "a saving that moves from the district's ledger to mine is not a saving; it is a transfer" (Source B). It would be easy to write her off as one frustrated parent, except that Source D found 41 percent of parents of children under 12 reported new childcare costs and 22 percent cut their own work hours. Source E shows the same split: 84 percent of teachers want to keep the calendar, but elementary parents are divided 48 to 42, and local employers, probably the people covering for those parents' missing hours, oppose it 49 to 37. The groups who like the schedule most are the ones it was designed to help, and the people closest to the youngest children are the ones paying for it.

That is why the conditions matter. Source D's achievement findings suggest the four-day schedule isn't the problem; lost hours are. Districts that kept total hours saw growth "statistically indistinguishable" from five-day districts, while those that cut hours fell 3 percentile points behind in math, mostly in grades 2 through 5. Pinemont Valley's third and fourth graders slipped in reading the first year, and the gap only closed after the district moved reading to the morning and paid for Friday tutoring (Source C). So a first-year dip doesn't prove the schedule fails, but a closed gap doesn't prove it works by itself either. Castellane's own summary, "We got lucky, and then we worked," reads less like a success story than a warning.

Even Pinemont hasn't solved childcare. Its enrichment day serves about 140 children at two of five buildings, paid for mostly by a county grant, and Castellane tells critics to "ask to see the waiting list." A district without that grant is not Pinemont. Harrow Fork has a library turning children away on Fridays and day-cares adding new rates, which suggests the town absorbed the cost instead of the district planning for it. Before a board copies Pinemont's results, it should ask whether it can copy Pinemont's repair work.

The four-day week is not a budget fix, and it is not a gift. It's a trade: teachers in exchange for a Friday that someone has to cover. A district that pays for that Friday itself has made a fair trade. A district that can't should take Source B's advice, raise the levy and pay teachers directly, because at least that puts the cost where everyone can see it.

A school district should only move to a four-day week if it is willing to keep the same number of instructional hours and provide care for families on Fridays. Without those two things, the schedule saves a little money but costs students and parents too much.

In Source A, Harrow Fork saved about 410,000 dollars, which is close to 2 percent of its budget. Source F shows that most of this came from transportation and utilities, and none of it came from teacher salaries. That means the savings are not very big, since salaries are the biggest cost. Source D agrees, saying no district reached the 5 percent that some expected. So if a district is only doing this to save money, it is probably not worth it.

Source A says Harrow Fork went from 14 unfilled positions to 5, and Source C says Pinemont Valley got eleven applicants for a job that used to get two. ALTON original passage
Commencement Address to the Dunmore Valley School of Nursing
Marisol Quenneville, charge nurse, Harrowgate Memorial Hospital night shift; commencement address delivered to the graduating class of the Dunmore Valley School of Nursing, 2019

¶1 (1) I have worked nights for nineteen years, and I will tell you the first thing the dark teaches: a hospital at three in the morning is never silent. (2) The monitors tick, the ice machine groans, somebody's call light blinks at the end of the hall like a slow pulse. (3) Most of that noise means nothing. (4) Some of it means everything. (5) The whole of our profession, I have come to believe, lives in the space between those two sentences.

¶2 (6) You have spent four years learning what to do. (7) You can run a line, titrate a drip, read a rhythm strip from across the room. (8) I am not here to add to that list. (9) I am here to talk about something that cannot be put on an exam: the discipline of paying attention. (10) I call it a discipline on purpose. (11) Attention is not a mood you fall into when the floor is quiet; it is a practice, like scrubbing in, that you perform the same way whether you feel like it or not.

¶3 (12) Let me tell you about a man in room 412. (13) This was my third year, and he was what we called a quiet patient, which is a dangerous compliment. (14) His vitals were fine. (15) His chart was fine. (16) He asked me, at twenty past two, whether I could open the blinds, and I nearly told him there was nothing out there but a parking lot. (17) Instead I asked him why. (18) He said he wanted to be able to see the sky in case he did not get another chance. (19) Nothing on the monitor had changed. (20) I called the resident anyway, and forty minutes later that man was in the cardiac unit, and he is, as far as I know, still alive, still looking at skies. (21) I did not save him with a skill. (22) I saved him by hearing a sentence.

¶4 (23) Now, I know what some of you are thinking, because I thought it too at your age. (24) You will have six patients, sometimes eight. (25) You will have a charting system that wants fourteen clicks to record a glass of water. (26) You will be tired in a way that has no name yet. (27) All of that is true, and I will not insult you by pretending otherwise. (28) But I have noticed, over nineteen years, that the nurses who miss things are not usually the busiest ones. (29) They are the ones who decided, somewhere along the way, that they already knew what they would find. (30) Fatigue takes your legs; certainty takes your eyes. (31) Of the two, certainty is the thief I fear.

¶5 (32) Our own quality committee at Harrowgate pulled the numbers last spring. (33) Of the seventy-one rapid-response calls on our medical floors last year, forty-four were triggered not by an alarm but by a nurse who simply reported that something was off. (34) Forty-four. (35) The machines, with all their sensors and their price tags, caught fewer than the people who were paying attention. (36) I do not say this to disparage the machines; they are good at what they measure. (37) I say it because what they do not measure is the thing you are being hired to notice.

¶6 (38) So here is what I ask of you, and it is small, and it is enormous. (39) When you walk into a room, stand still for three seconds before you touch anything. (40) Look at the hands, look at the breathing, look at what the patient is looking at. (41) Ask the second question. (42) The first question gets you a chart; the second gets you a person. (43) You will not do this perfectly. (44) I do not do it perfectly, and I have had nineteen years of practice. (45) But do it on purpose, every shift, until it stops being something you do and becomes something you are. (46) The hall will be loud tonight and every night after. (47) Listen anyway. (48) Congratulations, and welcome to the work.

parts.prompt:
Speaker: Marisol Quenneville, a charge nurse who has worked the overnight shift at the fictional Harrowgate Memorial Hospital for nineteen years. Audience: the graduating class of the fictional Dunmore Valley School of Nursing, their families, and faculty, gathered at a commencement ceremony. Exigence: the graduates have finished technical training and are about to begin work on understaffed floors where they will be tempted to rely on monitors and routine; Quenneville has been invited to give the commencement address. Purpose: to persuade the new nurses that attention is a deliberate, practiced discipline rather than a mood, and to convince them to commit to noticing patients as people even under exhausting conditions.

The passage below is a commencement address delivered in 2019 by Marisol Quenneville, a night-shift charge nurse at Harrowgate Memorial Hospital, to the graduating class of the Dunmore Valley School of Nursing. Read the passage carefully. Write an essay that analyzes the rhetorical choices Quenneville makes to convince the new graduates that paying attention is a discipline they must practice deliberately.

Your essay should:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible analysis of the rhetorical choices Quenneville makes.
- Select and use evidence from the passage to support your line of reasoning.
- Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning by showing how specific choices advance Quenneville's purpose for this audience and occasion.
parts.model_answer:
Most graduation speakers tell the audience they are ready. Marisol Quenneville, a night-shift charge nurse speaking to new nurses, has a harder job: she has to respect the four years of skills they just earned while telling them those skills are not what will matter most at three in the morning. She handles this by moving the graduates from a scene, to a story, to a statistic, and finally to a direct charge, and at each step she narrows what "attention" means until it is no longer a feeling but a habit they can perform. Most importantly, she concedes the exhaustion waiting for them so she can move the real danger somewhere they did not expect, from fatigue to certainty.

Quenneville opens with a sound instead of advice. The monitors "tick," the ice machine "groans," and a call light blinks "like a slow pulse." For an audience that has only done clinicals, this puts them on the floor before she asks anything of them, and the simile is telling, because even the background noise is given a heartbeat. Then she splits it: "Most of that noise means nothing. Some of it means everything." Those two short sentences set up the problem the whole speech tries to solve, which is how to tell the difference. Only after that does she define her term, calling attention "a practice, like scrubbing in." This comparison is chosen for nurses specifically. Scrubbing in is something they have done hundreds of times no matter their mood, so she borrows a habit they already respect and attaches attention to it.

The story of the man in room 412 then shows what this practice looks like. Quenneville uses flat, repeated sentences, "His vitals were fine. His chart was fine," that sound like the reassuring data a tired nurse would accept. The repetition makes the twist hit harder: the only warning sign was a request to see the sky. She also admits she "nearly told him there was nothing out there but a parking lot," which matters because she isn't posing as a hero with perfect instincts. She was a third-year nurse, not far from where the graduates are now. Her conclusion, "I did not save him with a skill. I saved him by hearing a sentence," answers her own second paragraph: skills are what they learned in school, but hearing is what she is asking for now.

She knows the graduates will push back, so she lists their objections for them. The "fourteen clicks to record a glass of water" is specific enough to be funny, and it shows she hasn't forgotten what the job is like. Because she promises "I will not insult you by pretending otherwise," her rebuttal lands harder: the nurses who miss things "decided, somewhere along the way, that they already knew what they would find." The line "Fatigue takes your legs; certainty takes your eyes" makes this memorable, but it is also a little uncomfortable for people who were just tested on knowing the answers. The confidence school rewarded is the "thief." Her hospital data backs this up, with forty-four of seventy-one rapid-response calls coming from a nurse who noticed "something was off," and repeating "Forty-four" alone forces the audience to sit with it. Still, she adds that machines "are good at what they measure." She is not telling them to ignore monitors, which would sound reckless with faculty in the room; she is telling them their job starts where the measuring stops.

By the last paragraph she has earned the right to give orders, and the tone shifts to imperatives: "stand still for three seconds," "Ask the second question." The request is concrete enough to try on a first shift. Her admission "I do not do it perfectly" keeps it from sounding like a lecture, and it actually supports her definition, since a discipline is something you never finish practicing. The ending brings back the opening scene: "The hall will be loud tonight and every night after. Listen anyway." The noise from the first paragraph hasn't gone away, and she doesn't pretend it will. Two words is all she leaves them with, which is about the right length for something to remember at three in the morning.

rubric_rows.criterion: Thesis must make an analytical claim about the relationship between at least one choice and the purpose (convincing new nurses that attention is a deliberate discipline). A thesis that argues Quenneville is 'effective' with no indication of how is not sufficient. A thesis that names devices but also asserts what they accomplish for this audience earns the point.

Choices that count include: the opening sensory description and simile (sentences 1 to 2); the antithesis 'Most of that noise means nothing. Some of it means everything' (3 to 4); the definition of attention as a discipline and the scrubbing-in simile (9 to 11); the room 412 anecdote with its short parallel sentences (12 to 22); the concession to workload and fatigue followed by the rebuttal that certainty, not busyness, causes misses (23 to 29); the metaphors 'Fatigue takes your legs; certainty takes your eyes' and 'certainty is the thief' (30 to 31); the hospital statistic and the one-word sentence 'Forty-four' (32 to 35); the qualification about machines (36 to 37); the shift to direct imperative instructions and a warmer tone (38 to 48); the closing two-word sentence 'Listen anyway' (47). Student commentary should connect choices to the specific audience: new graduates proud of technical skill who are about to be overwhelmed. Device labels are not required if the student describes the choice accurately.

Do not award for merely using sophisticated vocabulary, for a long introduction about nursing in general, or for a single clever sentence in the conclusion. The point is for thinking carried through the essay.
